caption:
6,811 likes, 31 comments - jesty_sunny on August 7, 2026: "The Psychology of Horror! 

Horror films have always held a unique place in cinema because they allow audiences to experience fear from the safety of a theater or living room. They tap into our deepest anxieties such as death, the unknown, isolation, and the supernatural, while offering the thrill of surviving those emotions without real danger. 

Psychologists have long tried to explain this fascination. The excitation transfer theory suggests that the fear and physiological arousal created during a horror film make the sense of relief and enjoyment afterward even more intense. The uses and gratifications theory proposes that people actively choose horror to seek excitement, emotional stimulation, or even a sense of mastery over fear. 

Others point to morbid curiosity, our natural tendency to explore danger and the unknown in a safe environment as well as sensation-seeking, where individuals with a higher need for novel and intense experiences are especially drawn to the genre. Together, these theories suggest that horror is not simply about being scared, it’s about satisfying deep psychological needs.

A great horror film is therefore more than jump scares. It creates atmosphere, psychological tension, and lingering unease while allowing audiences to confront fear without real-world consequences.

Which is your favourite horror film?

#horror #cinema #thriller #obsession #backrooms".

Pattachitra is one of my favourite art forms, maybe because of its intricate detailing and the way all those tiny elements come together to create such a gorgeous final piece.

Patta means cloth and chitra means painting, so Pattachitra literally refers to a painting made on a prepared cloth surface.

And making the patt itself is a process. Traditionally, two layers of cloth are joined with tamarind seed gum, followed by a layer of chalk powder mixed with the same adhesive. Once dry, it is sanded and polished to create a smooth surface for painting. I tried this process on an MDF board instead of making it directly on the floor, so I can either remove the artwork later or keep it on the board as it is.

Traditionally, natural colours are used, made from sources like geru, haritala, lamp soot, chalk and conch shell. I used acrylics for this piece, while trying to retain the traditional Pattachitra-inspired detailing.

She doesn't want to defeat her husband-she simply wants the freedom to remain herself after marriage. At the same time, Veera's journey forces him to confront his own ego and understand that having a strong, ambitious wife doesn't make a husband weaker.

Their relationship gradually becomes a story about respect, acceptance, and learning to support the person you love instead of controlling them.

What made Rivers special was his ability to operate as a true field general. He constantly changed protections, identified blitzes, adjusted routes at the line of scrimmage, and trusted his football IQ to beat defenses. While today’s quarterbacks are more athletic than ever, players who can consistently diagnose defenses, command the line of scrimmage, and win with anticipation and football intelligence alone are becoming increasingly rare. pointless_existence._ on August 4, 2026: "A real relationship was never meant to be measured by how often you hold someone’s hand, but by how safely they can hold your heart.

Love isn’t just flowers, late-night calls, hugs, kisses, or photos together. Those are beautiful moments, but they aren’t the foundation. The strongest relationships are built on the things people don’t always see—trust that doesn’t need constant reassurance, loyalty that stays even during difficult times, respect during disagreements, patience during silence, and support when life feels heavy.

A healthy relationship is having someone who listens without judging, stays without being asked, and chooses you even on the days when you’re not easy to love. It’s knowing that no matter how far life pulls you apart, you’re still a team.

Real love isn’t perfect. It has misunderstandings, bad days, distance, and challenges. But when two people genuinely care for each other, they don’t look for reasons to leave—they look for reasons to stay, communicate, and grow together.

The right person won’t just celebrate your happiest moments. They’ll stand beside you when you’re struggling, remind you of your worth when you forget it, and make you feel at home even in the middle of chaos.

At the end of the day, the best relationships aren’t loud. They are peaceful. They feel safe, honest, and effortless because they’re built on love, trust, care, respect, and loyalty—not just attraction.

If you have someone like that in your life, value them. Genuine connections are becoming rare, and the people who love you with consistency are worth holding onto.

Stop shrinking your personality just to fit into places where you don’t belong. Stop lowering your standards just to keep people comfortable. • 1 litre regular milk
• 2 cups jaggery

✨ Pour the mixture into a cooker-safe tin.
✨ Steam in a pressure cooker for 3–4 whistles.
✨ Let it cool to room temperature.
✨ Refrigerate for 4–5 hours.

Ghewar Batter
• 1½ cups maida
• ¼ cup melted ghee
• 3–4 ice cubes
• 2–2½ cups ice-cold water

Whisk the ghee and ice by hand until light, fluffy and pale. Mix in the maida, then gradually add the ice-cold water to make a smooth, thin batter. Pour the batter into hot ghee from a height in several rounds to create the signature honeycomb texture. Fry until crisp and golden.

Sugar Syrup
• 1 cup sugar
• ½ cup water
• Few saffron strands
• ¼ tsp cardamom powder

Boil until the sugar dissolves completely.

Rabdi
• 1 litre full-fat milk
• 3–4 tbsp sugar
• Few saffron strands
• ¼ tsp cardamom powder
• Chopped pistachios & almonds

Reduce the milk to one-third, stir in the sugar, saffron and cardamom until thick and creamy.

Pour obtenir la forme complète, j’ai dû faire monter le drone jusqu’à près de 500 mètres d’altitude, puis assembler un panorama de neuf photos. C’est seulement en post-production que ce « fossile » est apparu dans son intégralité.

Le plus drôle, c’est que cette histoire ne concerne que la première photo de ce carrousel. Derrière chacune des autres se cache aussi une anecdote, un réveil beaucoup trop tôt, plusieurs heures de piste ou une lumière qui n’a duré que quelques minutes. 

C’est fou de se dire qu’il y a une histoire derrière chacun de ces clichés. Je n’aurai malheureusement jamais assez de place pour toutes vous les raconter. Une prochaine fois peut-être 🌝____

caption:
samhorine on August 14, 2026: "Ballard on a Sunday doing that classic Seattle thing where it’s cloudy in the morning and then by 11am or so it burns off and you end up with what most people would consider the ideal summer day at mostly sunny, no humidity and +/- 80° (26° Celsius for my classy friends) 

Ballard is a cool neighborhood and I could write pages and pages about its history with annotated slides and such but hey, this is Instagzam not the history channel so instead please enjoy the photos and this short bit about how Ballard was once the shingle capital of the west👇🏻

“After the Great Seattle Fire in 1889 the Ballard mills provided opportunities for those who had lost jobs in the fire, which in turn spurred the growth of the settlement as families moved north to work in the mills. Ballard’s first mill, built in 1888 by Mr. J Sinclair was a lumber mill; the second, finished the same year was a shingle mill. The local western red cedar’s wood was extremely well-suited to the creation of shingles, and Ballard quickly became the center of shingle production in the region, earning the nicknames “Shingletown” and the “Shingle Capital of America.” Ballard High School’s mascot was the Shingle Weavers until the 1950s, when it switched to the Beavers, referencing the timber industry more generally. Ballard experienced an influx of Scandinavian immigrants during this period, and Scandinavian culture and traditions would be influential on Ballard as it developed into its own distinct waterfront neighborhood”".

145 likes, 7 comments - michaelrallen on August 13, 2026: "One of the joys of the last year was receiving a research grant from @wvuhumanities that seriously expedited the development of my book project, Another Modernism: Mass Housing, Architectural History and the Promise of Justice. In fact, because of the grant, I was able to finish the development and submission of a full manuscript proposal this summer.
 
Another Modernism builds out from my research project that examines the politics of expertise in the valuation of US mass housing as the subject of architectural history and historic preservation. Credentialed experts have reproduced tremendous implicit race, class and gender biases that have silenced, stigmatized and omitted the most prevalent form of global twentieth century multifamily housing from American architectural history. Yet inhabitants have fought for this architecture, sometimes for aesthetic value but often for other reasons – and they have transformed their dwellings and buildings in ways that experts have considered blows to “integrity” when in fact these demonstrate agency and co-making. Fundamental questions: Who decides what is architectural history, and how? Do architectural history and historic preservation offer any meaningful empowerment to mass housing residents fighting against demolition and displacement today?
 
My work explores the Cochran Gardens public housing project in St. Louis (built 1953 / demolished 2002-2012) and the Parkchester private low-rent housing project in the Bronx, New York City (built 1938-42). The grant allowed me to travel to make some long stops at archives and obtain a set of interviews, including one I had been trying to schedule for three years.
 
Having research support for humanities scholars at a land-grant university is crucial and critical right now in the face of a bad-faith attack on our work. May @wvuhumanities continue funding timely, vital research and may I get this book under contract soon.".

caption: 442 likes, 16 comments - chaseburnett_ on July 24, 2026: "Ellen and Barbara. Two incredible people giving it their all to manage and conserve nearly six million acres of Forest Service Land in Alaska. Our mission this trip: Shrode Lake Cabin trail maintenance. Tucked away in Prince William Sound, the journey to Shrode Lake is remote, beautiful, and humbling. This trip has historically been one of the wetter trips on the summer roster, and our stint was no different. Out of our four days in the sound, there were only a few hours of reprieve from the unrelenting downpour. The saying goes “come hell or high water”. Well, we definitely had high water. Among the towering trees, lush meadows, and inlets teeming with life, the most striking thing to me was Ellen and Barbara’s commitment to the mission. Joined by volunteers through the Prince William Sound Stewardship Foundation, Ellen and Barbara guided our efforts to transport tools, improve trail conditions, and perform cabin maintenance. Anyone who has been in the sound will tell you it’s a special place. But its importance takes on a greater meaning when you witness the effort and dedication necessary to provide responsible access to some of its remote corners. The work they do is important, and I’m frustrated at the reality of small men making decisions in a dry boardroom that impact the people willing to get out there in a torrential downpour to ensure this land is protected. This work deserves more support than I think it will get in the near future. The very fact that I have the opportunity to write about this unique experience is a testament to the importance of responsible and sustainable access to Prince William Sound. More from this trip is now live on my Journal.".

	●	1 kg chicken, cut into medium pieces
	●	15 almonds
	●	15 cashews
	●	½ cup desiccated coconut

	●	2 tsp red chili powder
	●	2 tsp garam masala
	●	1 tsp coriander powder
	●	1 tsp cumin powder
	●	1 tbsp chicken masala (store-bought)
	●	½ tsp turmeric powder
	●	Juice of 1 lemon
	●	1 tbsp red chili sauce (Indian-style)
	●	1 tbsp green chili sauce (Indian-style)
	●	1 tbsp soy sauce
	●	1 tbsp tomato paste or tomato purée
	●	4–5 green chilies, slit
	●	2 large onions, fried
	●	Fresh mint, chopped

	●	1–2 tbsp heavy cream
	●	Oil, as needed

	1.	Grind the almonds, cashews, and desiccated coconut into a fine paste.

caption:
kevinrjamieson on August 6, 2026: "My final day of visiting Vancouver’s World Cup.   I started with an errand outside the downtown core. Walking back into the city it was a stark reminder that not all things are right in the world, or in the city. Unhoused folks, active drug use, mental disorders… all on display as I made my way to Granville street. I don’t think there is a way to fully reconcile the disparity between the struggles of individuals living in the streets and the significant spend shouldered by the tax payers. While there is certainly good that came from the World Cup hosting, does it out weigh the potential spend to provide support for those in need? A question I can’t answer, but certainly one I pondered. 

What I do know… Many many people embraced the World Cup. Those same people came out in support of their countries teams, and brought excitement and energy into the street. Families came out and shared experiences together. Strangers made friends. Fun was had.".

105 likes, 5 comments - cindywinterfeldt on July 30, 2026: "📖 Storyfold – Schattenwald

🧭 Fakten 

👤 1 Person
⏱️ 30–60 Minuten pro Partie
📚 über 10 Stunden Kampagne
🎂 ab 12 Jahren

🗺️ Worum geht’s?

In Storyfold – Schattenwald begleitet ihr Luma und ihren Bären Brom auf ihrer Reise durch den geheimnisvollen Schattenwald. Gemeinsam versucht ihr, den Wald von den bedrohlichen Schatten zu befreien. Dabei trefft ihr Entscheidungen, erkundet neue Orte und erlebt die Geschichte Kapitel für Kapitel. 

Das Besondere: Dank des Prologs könnt ihr direkt losspielen. Die Regeln lernt ihr ganz nebenbei während des Spiels kennen. Genau so wünsche ich mir den Einstieg in ein Storyspiel.

⛵ Besonders spannend

Die Fluss-Mechanik hat mir richtig gut gefallen. Ich musste immer wieder überlegen, wann ich welche Karten einsetze und wie ich meine Würfel am sinnvollsten nutze. Das fühlt sich einfach richtig rund an.

Dazu kommt das Artwork. Ganz ehrlich: Selten hat mich ein Spiel optisch so begeistert. Jede Seite des Storybooks wirkt wie aus einem Märchenbuch und macht die Atmosphäre einfach unglaublich dicht.

🚩 Mein Ersteindruck

Die Geschichte rund um Luma und Brom hat mich von Anfang an mitgenommen. Ich wollte nach jedem Abschnitt wissen, wie es weitergeht und was die beiden als Nächstes erwartet.

Nach dem ersten Kapitel musste ich nur aufhören, weil es schon spät war. Ansonsten hätte ich direkt weitergespielt.

Für mich zeigt das, wie gut das Spiel funktioniert: Es lebt nicht nur von seinen Mechaniken, sondern vor allem von seiner Geschichte und der Atmosphäre.

Durch den Einsatz der Würfel gehört auch etwas Glück dazu, aber durch bestimmte Karten kann man da dem Glück etwas nachhelfen. 

🏆 Fazit

Storyfold – Schattenwald gehört für mich zu den atmosphärischsten Solospielen, die ich bisher gespielt habe.

Das wunderschöne Artwork, der gelungene Einstieg ohne Regelstudium und die Geschichte rund um Luma und Brom haben mich komplett in ihren Bann gezogen. Ich freue mich schon jetzt darauf, die nächsten Kapitel zu erleben.

Werbung I reduziertes Rezensionsexemplar von @boardgamecircus 

❓Welches Solospiel hat euch zuletzt so gefesselt, dass ihr unbedingt wissen musstet, wie die Geschichte weitergeht?".

22K likes, 374 comments - tedgorephotography on November 30, 2020: "New shot! New videos! Cybermonday deal! 

Yeah… crazy. I know, I haven’t put out anything new in quite a while, but… that’s a long story, maybe for another time. Rather than get into where I’ve been and why I’ve been there, I’ll just share this shot that I’ve had sitting around on my dusty hard drives for quite awhile… along with others! Maybe I will get around to releasing those as well some day. 

I took this in Death Valley several years ago while leading a workshop, and it was one of the coolest displays of light I think I’ve ever seen. This beam of light developed and evolved over the span of a couple hours. I have some other shots from longer focal lengths of the more intimate scenes it was creating with the mountain side off in the distance that are pretty cool too. This is a pretty common mud playa that many people shoot from these days, but I really liked how this mud crack in the FG traveled around and through the scene to link up with the beam of light. Not the best composition I’ve ever created, but the light was the real show and I just needed something to showcase it a bit, and I’m happy to have something to remember this night from. 

So this year has been a crazy one! Back over the summer I took a few months to create a whole bunch of new video content. Seemed like a good time to focus on something like that. It will all be released on a new dedicated tutorial website that I’m having created. It’s not quite ready, but the videos are, and I figured Cyber Monday would be a good opportunity to put them out there and let some of you all snag them at a discounted price. I have 3 videos I’m releasing. A new start-to-finish style video for one of my images from the Dolomites, Purple Poison, a video on color theory for landscape photography, and a video on composition for landscape photography. 

If you’re interested in picking those up, or any of my other videos, I have a 33% off deal going by using the code CYBERMONDAY2020, or if you buy 5 or more videos, you can get 50% off using the code CM2020FIVE.

You can find the new videos at the link in my profile.

Thanks!".

641 likes, 5 comments - arkular_ on August 16, 2026: "Architecture to inspire. House on Sag Harbor by @1100architect is a study in restraint: a quietly commanding home for an acclaimed American ceramicist, carefully sited and pared back to let the landscape take the lead.

From the outset, the home was set roughly 60 metres back from the shoreline, almost three times the minimum required. It’s a decision that puts ecology, space and long-term resilience ahead of simply getting closer to the water. It also looks ahead to tougher coastal conditions and rising sea levels.

Internally, the home is organised around two perpendicular wings, creating an L-shaped plan that keeps social spaces distinct while making the whole house easy to move through. Expanses of glass pull in light and landscape, while a 12-metre living room opening disappears completely, letting the breeze, bay and outdoors straight in.

How will House on Sag Harbor read 100 years from now? The ambition is simple: a home that lasts, emotionally engaging, adaptable in how it separates public and private life, and resilient enough to stand the test of time.

cecphotos on August 11, 2026: "A fresh look at an old favorite. 🌊✨

Every now and then, I like to go back into the archives and re-process frames that held a lot of personal meaning. As our eye for light and editing style evolves over time, going back with fresh eyes can bring out a completely different energy in a shot.

With this coastal long exposure, my focus was on refining the textures and bringing back a clean, natural balance. By cooling down the water tones and dialing in the contrast, it allowed the dynamic wave motion and leading lines in the foreground to truly take center stage. 2,874 likes, 43 comments - kotovich on August 13, 2026: "Ну вот и прошло затмение. Теперь можно спокойно выдохнуть и разбирать отснятое.

Скажу сразу: сомнения, ехать или нет, были до последнего. Ещё днём шёл дождь. И хотя мой прогноз выглядел оптимистично, но облака явно не собирались облегчать жизнь фотографам. 

Но тут у меня правило простое: если есть хотя бы небольшой шанс — лучше ехать. Не получится — значит получишь опыт и в следующий раз будешь лучше понимать, что делать в похожих условиях. А вот сидеть дома и потом смотреть, как у кого-то между облаками всё-таки показалось Солнце, гораздо обиднее.

С той облачностью, которая была над Петербургом, никаких совсем уж сложных задумок я себе не ставил. В чат я уже накидал что наснимали иностранные коллеги и это шикарно. правда и затмение у них полное было. А для себя задача была простой: снять небольшую секвенцию затмения и вписать её в город.

Поэтому я не пытался совместить Солнце с какой-то одной доминантой. Наоборот, выбирал точку так, чтобы вся траектория заходящего Солнца нормально легла в кадр и стала частью композиции.

Насколько получилось — судить уже зрителю. Но я точно получил удовольствие и от самой съёмки, и от компании. А это, как ни крути, тоже довольно важная часть процесса :)

Финальный кадр собран таймблендингом — то есть город и разные положения Солнца сняты в разное время и объединены в одной фотографии. При этом каждый исходный кадр снимал брекетингом из пяти кадров с шагом в 1 стоп, чтобы не пережечь солнце ине провалить город.

Отдельные кадры и промежуточные варианты положу в комментарии.

1,759 likes, 21 comments - deathvalleynps on July 15, 2026: "What’s in a name? 
 
People often think that Death Valley received its forbidding name from the extreme summertime heat the park is most known for, but the name actually came from a group of lost ’49-ers. These pioneers, lured west by the hope of fortune and a better life after the discovery of gold in California in 1848, were tempted by the prospect of the shortcut, but instead ended up lost here in the winter of 1849-1850. 
 
As far as records show, only one member of that party died during their ordeal here, but the group certainly thought they would meet their untimely demise. When they were rescued by two of the party’s men, John Rogers and William Lewis Manly, the group made their way west of mountains. It is said that one member of the party proclaimed, “Goodbye Death Valley,” giving the valley its morbid name. 
 
This ominous naming scheme is reflected throughout the park with names like Funeral Peak and Deadman Pass, and Dante’s View. But despite the harsh names applied to Death Valley by pioneers, miners, and early tourism promoters, Death Valley is full of life boasting over 1,000 plant species and 440 animal species! 

📍 Dante's View 

Alt Text: Color photo of a low basin and salt flats with mountains on either side taken from above. NPS".

caption:
4,532 likes, 82 comments - oscarniemeyerworks on May 1, 2026: "Oscar Niemeyer cultivou ao longo da vida uma paixão pelo futebol — sobretudo pelo Fluminense. Não por acaso: o clube, historicamente associado à elite carioca, tem sede em Laranjeiras, bairro onde ele cresceu. Niemeyer permaneceu torcedor fiel ao longo de toda a vida.

Pouca gente sabe, mas na infância ele chegou a jogar pelo Fluminense. Registros históricos do clube documentam sua participação em uma partida em 14 de julho de 1918, quando, com apenas 11 anos, atuou como meio-campista - eles perderam por 4 a 0.

Em 1945, ele foi contratado para projetar um novo edifício para o Iate Clube Fluminense, a ser construído à beira-mar, na Avenida Pasteur, conectando Botafogo à Urca. Não se sabe muito sobre o esquema geral do conjunto, mas desenhos sugerem que ele também contaria com hangares destinados a hidroaviões.

O projeto não foi construído, mas ganhou destaque na historiografia. Em 2012, Peter Buchanan, escrevendo para a Architectural Review, destacou o edifício como um grande exemplo de planta livre. Segundo ele, a qualidade desse tipo de espaço está no equilíbrio: poucos elementos, cuidadosamente posicionados, são suficientes para sugerir usos e organizar as atividades sem determiná-las em excesso.

No caso do iate clube, um espaço retangular sob uma cobertura suavemente curva é articulado de forma mínima, mas precisa, para acomodar diferentes usos em sequência e em relação entre si. Muitos dos elementos são curvos, contribuindo para o dinamismo do ambiente e para a forma como conduzem o movimento das pessoas.

Ao chegar ao topo da rampa, o mar se revela à frente. Seguindo adiante, surge uma vista descendente dos iates ancorados por meio de uma abertura no piso. À direita, um lounge com áreas mais íntimas, distribuídas acima e abaixo de uma galeria. À esquerda, uma parede curva orienta o percurso entre o bar e as mesas voltadas para a baía, conduzindo, de forma gradual e coreografada, ao centro do restaurante.".

We moved to southwestern Colorado because of these mountains and they hold many of our favorite places – that stand of particularly elegant old aspens, the most luscious corn lily patch around, the fascinating geology, the higher trails into fields of summer wildflowers, the rainbow patchwork of oaks in the fall, and so much more. 

My brain knows that this ecosystem needs fire but I’m feeling pretty heartbroken over it all right now. With lower winds and less smoke today, we have been able to see more of what is happening but it is still hard to tell what has and has not burned because the topography of the area is so complex with all the drainages and ridges. The most active part of the fire, from our vantage point, is burning through Gambel oak right now, with dark black smoke billowing up with each new patch going up in flames. The huge firefighting response has, so far, kept the towns and most structures safe but the forecast continues to leave extreme uncertainty in terms of what is to come and the fire is moving toward many homes and ranches. 

These snapshot photos are mostly of the area right below Chimney Peak and Courthouse Mountain, with a few to the south toward Baldy Peak, taken on July 3 with a telephoto lens. I included some similar photos so you can see how much the fire and smoke are moving around across twenty to thirty minutes. Bonus teeny tiny helicopter included in one for scale. #goldmountainfire #ouray #ridgway".

4,505 likes, 83 comments - elialocardi on February 23, 2026: "Seeing Old Photos in a New Light 📸✨

As photographers, we’re always chasing the next shot, but sometimes our best images are already waiting—buried in old folders, unseen for years. For 15 years, I’ve traveled, waited for perfect light, and captured moments that meant everything then... only to leave many of them untouched, filed away for “later.”

As photographers, our passion often lies in our newest work. But what if our greatest images, waiting to be rediscovered, were captured years ago—like in 2011 and 2012?

Why? Because our skills and perspectives evolve. We look at old work and see flaws instead of potential. But recently, while digging through my archives, I realized something: when we revisit our past work, we see it with new eyes. We’re not judging our old selves—we’re collaborating with them.

Some photos I’d forgotten turned out to be hidden gems, needing just a few tweaks with today’s tools to shine. Technology like Radiant Photo makes finishing what I started years ago so much easier—no more endless slider-wrangling.

Maybe your future favorite photo is already on your hard drive. Give your archives a second look. You might rediscover not just powerful images, but also your own creative growth. 🔥

What’s the best shot you’ve ever found in your archives? Share your story below! 👇".

caption:
932 likes, 45 comments - chrisbyrnephotography on August 14, 2026: "My latest crop of aerial images from Iceland photographed last month. It was an absolute thrill getting my workshop clients up in a plane over these braided rivers. I’ve been fortunate enough to do this on nearly all of my trips over there since my first flight in 2018 and it simply never gets old. And to see it through the fresh and excited eyes of my guests is something even more special. We had excellent conditions and the river systems in the south were quite beautiful on this day with their endless tendrils and abstract patterns. It’s a subject I love to shoot and will beat to death for as long as I can. 

It’s been quite awhile since I’ve shared any actual work over here as my summer has been spent in construction mode and other projects. I’ve certainly posted more videos of my ugly mug in the last two months than I have in the ten years prior with the progress of how that’s all going. Anyway I hope that you all enjoy this set and many thanks for checking out my work!".

Among hunting spiders in particular, this strategy helps ensure the female focuses on the provided prey instead of immediately attacking her potential mate after copulation.

caption:
1,596 likes, 11 comments - mecanoo_ on July 21, 2026: "Mecanoo shapes Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi as a geological landscape

The Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi is the largest natural history museum in the Middle East and a new cultural and scientific destination within Saadiyat Cultural District. Conceived as a landscape rather than a singular architectural object, the museum brings together architecture, nature and public space in an immersive environment for discovery.

Inspired by the geological formations and wadis of the region, the building emerges from the landscape as a series of sculpted volumes. Public pathways, terraces and shaded spaces invite visitors to explore the site before entering the museum, extending the experience beyond its galleries and into the public realm.

At its heart, a monumental entrance lobby introduces visitors to the scale and ambition of the museum, while exhibitions unfold as a continuous journey through the history of the natural world, from the origins of the universe to the challenges facing our planet today. Organised around a central courtyard, the galleries encourage both guided exploration and personal discovery.

Designed for both the public and the scientific community, the museum combines exhibitions, education and research within one accessible institution. More than a place to preserve knowledge, it creates opportunities for learning, dialogue and shared discovery, strengthening the connection between architecture, landscape and science.

Mecanoo, Egis, Broadway Malyan, Pascall+Watson, WAHO Landscape Architects, Plan A Consultants, EllisDon, Miral, DCT (Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi).

📷 by @ossipvanduivenbode

Read more at mecanoo.nl
#architecture #design #mecanoo".

caption:
startupsunboxing on August 4, 2026: "5 Wholesale Markets Where India's Clothing Businesses Actually Buy Stock

Most people think a clothing business is won on Instagram. It's actually won at the source, the place you buy your stock.
Here's the truth nobody tells beginners. Two sellers can sell the exact same kurti. One buys it for ₹250 and the other for ₹180. Same product, same price to the customer, but one makes far more profit on every single order. That difference is not luck. It's sourcing. And India has a handful of wholesale hubs where the real money is made before you sell a single piece.

1. Surat, Gujarat, the fabric and ethnic wear capital.
Surat is India's largest textile hub, and it's the number one choice for Meesho and Instagram sellers. You buy synthetic dress material, sarees, and lehenga fabric straight from manufacturers, which means almost no middlemen and better margins. If you sell women's ethnic wear online, this is usually where your journey begins.

2. Gandhi Nagar, Delhi, the readymade garment king.
When you want finished clothes ready to sell, Gandhi Nagar is hard to beat. It's India's biggest readymade garment market, offering ethnic, western, and everyday wear in massive variety. Nearby, Sadar Bazaar and Chandni Chowk give you some of the cheapest budget and street fashion in the country.

3. Tirupur, Tamil Nadu, the knitwear powerhouse.
Tirupur is India's knitwear and T-shirt capital, and a major export cluster. If you sell T-shirts, sweatshirts, or cotton basics, this gives you factory-direct prices that are almost impossible to match elsewhere, especially when you buy in volume.

4. Kolkata, Burrabazar, the lowest rates at scale.
Burrabazar is known for some of the cheapest wholesale clothing in India. If your business runs on thin margins and high volume, this is a serious sourcing option worth the trip.

5. Ludhiana, Punjab, the winter wear hub.
Ludhiana is India's hosiery and woollen capital. Sweaters, thermals, and winter clothing are cheapest and most reliable here, so if your sales spike in winter, this is your market.

#clothingbusiness #wholesalemarket #startupindia #businessideas #reselling smallbusiness entrepreneurindia boutiquebusiness meeshoseller t".

The order, under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, also prohibits hotels, restaurants, caterers, and cloud kitchens from using or serving this product.

attitudeslides on July 28, 2026: "7 Weird Ways to Control Your Mind

Your mind is either your greatest strength or your biggest obstacle. The good news is that you can train it with a few simple habits.

1. The Double Breath: Take two quick breaths in, then slowly breathe out. A longer exhale tells your body it’s safe, helping you feel calm almost instantly.

2. Name It to Tame It: When emotions hit, identify them. Saying, “I’m anxious” or “I’m frustrated” reduces their power and helps you think clearly.

3. Cold on Command: Take cold showers regularly. Learning to stay relaxed through small discomfort builds resilience for bigger challenges.

4. Posture Rewires You: Sit or stand tall with your shoulders back. Strong posture influences your mindset, making you feel more confident and focused.

5. Rehearse It Real: Visualize success before taking action. Your brain treats vivid mental practice almost like real experience, improving confidence and performance.

6. Widen Your Eyes: Relax your gaze and notice more of your surroundings. A wider visual focus signals safety, reducing stress and improving awareness.

7. Move to Think: Whenever you feel stuck, start moving. Walk, stretch, or exercise for a few minutes. Movement boosts blood flow, clears mental fog, and helps you regain control of your thoughts.

Creamy Thecha Mushroom

Recipe: 

Ingredients: 
 
For the thecha:

8-10 garlic cloves 
1/4 cup peanuts 
1 tbsp oil 
1 tsp jeera 
1 cup fresh coriander 
Salt to taste

Other ingredients: 
1 tbsp butter
2 packs of mushroom (400 gms) 
1/2 to 1 cup fresh cream (based on preference) 

Process: 
In a pan, add whole green chillies, garlic cloves, peanuts and toast for 2-3 minutes until they start turning light golden brown 

Add some oil and jeera, cook for another 2-3 minutes 

Transfer to a mortal pastel, add some fresh coriander and salt, grind to form a coarse paste. Alternatively, you can also grind using a mixer grinder 

In a pan, add some butter, little oil and whole mushrooms, cook until the mushrooms turn golden brown from the bottom and are cooked, add salt to taste and mix

12K likes, 65 comments - side_end_developer__ on August 5, 2026: "Japan’s Maglev train doesn’t touch the track. It floats 10cm above it. No wheels. No friction. 600 km/h. Here’s the engineering. 
Maglev has two fundamental problems to solve — how to keep the train floating against gravity, and how to move it forward without wheels. Both are solved by magnets — in different ways. 
The train carries superconducting magnets cooled by liquid helium to minus 269 degrees — almost absolute zero — the same temperature as outer space. At this temperature electrical resistance drops to zero and these magnets generate a magnetic field 10 times more powerful than normal magnets. Same superconducting magnet technology used in India’s hydrogen train. 
Up to 140 km/h the train runs on wheels. Beyond that the superconducting magnets pass rapidly alongside figure-8 shaped coils embedded in the guideway. This moving magnetic field induces eddy currents in those coils — Faraday’s Law — the same principle behind NFC card payments and hydrogen fuel cells. These eddy currents create their own magnetic field that repels the train’s magnets upward. Train rises 10cm. Wheels retract. Zero contact. Zero friction. 
For propulsion — three phase AC electromagnets in the guideway energize in sequence creating a traveling magnetic wave moving forward. The train’s magnets are pushed and pulled by this wave — moving forward. Speed up — wave faster. Brake — wave reverses — energy fed back to the grid. No engine. No moving parts. Pure magnetic force. 
Faraday’s Law — discovered in 1831 — powers your NFC card payment, India’s hydrogen train, and levitates the world’s fastest train. Same physics. Three completely different applications.
Japan’s SCMaglev hit 603 km/h in 2015. Without touching the track. Just magnetic force. Floating.

#collegestudents #maglev #japanmaglev #maglevtrain #trains".

9,918 likes, 78 comments - tasteatlas on June 25, 2026: "Indian Milk Cake (Alwar Ka Mawa) by @khatrisweetsraipur 
 📍 Raipur, India 🇮🇳

Making authentic Indian sweets, known locally as mithai, is a true masterclass in patience. One of the most beloved traditional treats is Milk Cake, famously known in India as Alwar ka Mawa or Kalakand. It requires hours of slow-cooking to achieve its iconic, irresistible texture.

The secret behind this fudge-like sweet is the continuous reduction of milk over steady heat. Halwais (traditional sweetmakers) boil the milk down for hours until the liquid evaporates, leaving behind a rich, solid milk mass. A touch of sugar, ghee, and a tiny hint of lemon juice are introduced to slightly curdle the mixture, giving it a uniquely grainy, crumbly, and juicy bite.

Once the thick mixture is transferred into deep containers, it is left to cool down very slowly. The intense residual heat trapped inside continues to cook the core of the block, naturally creating a beautiful two-toned appearance with a deeply caramelized, darker brown center. After completely setting, the massive blocks are sliced into perfect rectangles, ready to be shared during major festivals and celebrations.".
